INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici Curiae’s lives have been irreparably and
violently impacted by civilians who wielded uniquely
destructive weapons of war in schools, grocery stores,
houses of worship, streets, and homes across the
country.  Amici profiled herein were present at or lost
loved ones in mass shootings perpetrated by assault
weapons.  As described in Appendix A, additional
listed amici have been directly affected by assault
weapons.
Having been devastated by the pain and suffering
that assault weapons inflict, amici have a substantial
interest in this Court recognizing that the Constitution
permits democratically-elected officials to protect the
health and safety of their communities and the lives of
their residents, and to regulate the purchase and use
of these weapons in their communities.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Assault weapons 2 are designed to be fast,
destructive, and easy -to-use, and have become

life-altering harm resulting from individual s using

ARGUMENT
I. ASSAULT WEAPONS ARE UNIQUELY
DESTRUCTIVE AND DESIGNED TO
EFFICIENTLY INFLICT MAXIMUM
HARM
Assault weapons are uniquely destructive firearms.
They are military -grade weapons that have several
features specific to distance combat and designed to
inflict maximum damage on targets.  These features
are what make assault weapons the guns of choice for

3 Included in this brief are narratives from those who were

civilians seeking to inflict harm on a large scale,
including catastrophic injury and mass murder.4
First, assault weapons fire bullets at an extremely
high velocity.  For example, an AR-15 propels a bullet
“at a speed that would cross six football fields in a
second.”5  Because speed provides a bullet with kinetic
energy, a bullet’s velocity is a “dominant factor” in the
amount of damage it can cause the human body. 6  At
impact, a bullet fired from an assault weapon like an
AR-15 creates a “blast effect” that causes damage to a
massive block of surrounding tissue, akin to the wake
that follows a boat speeding through water. 7
Observers of victims of assault weapons commonly

Second, assault weapons can be fired at an
extremely rapid rate, dramatically increasing their
lethality.  The average semiautomatic assault rifle can
fire up to 45 rounds per minute. 11  As a result,
significant damage can be inflicted in an extremely
short period of time.  For example:
• In 2019, a shooter using an assault weapon
killed nine people and injured 27 others in
just 32 seconds in Dayton, Ohio.12
• In 2022, a shooter using an assault weapon
fired 60 shots in just over two minutes in a
grocery store in Buffalo, New York, killing
ten and injuring three.13
• In 1989, a shooter using an assault weapon
fired over 100 rounds within three minutes
at an elementary school in Stockton,
California, killing five children and injuring
30.  News media reported that “the yard at

Third, assault weapons are relatively easy to use,
even by someone with little  or no firearm experience,
and are specifically designed for accuracy .  Among
other features, assault weapons mitigate recoil,
resulting in the shooter’s aim being disturbed less
between shots, allowing for rapid follow -up fire on a
target.15
The combination of these features —the speed at
which bullets travel and can be fired and their relative
ease of use —makes assault weapons uniquely
destructive.16  Unlike other firearms, they are
specifically designed to kill large numbers of people
quickly and thus are particularly lethal. 17  They are,
quite literally, weapons of war.18

Because assault weapons are so uniquely
destructive and comparatively easy to use, they have
increasingly become the weapon of choice for
individuals seeking to indiscriminately inflict as much
harm as possible, with devastating results.  The use of
assault weapons has risen at an alarming rate in the
last two decades.   Shooters chose assault weapons in
34% of mass shootings in the 2010s and 60% in the
2020s, up from 17 -20% from the 1970s through the
2000s.19  The use of assault weapons has led to 55%
more fatalities  in mass shootings  and roughly four
times as many injuries. 20  And the number of mass
shootings involving the use of an assault weapon in the
last 15 years is higher than the total number of mass
shootings for each of the prior decades , going back to
the 1960s.21

II. THE EXPERIENCES OF SURVIVORS OF
MASS SHOOTINGS WITH ASSAULT
WEAPONS DEMONSTRATE THEIR
DANGER AND LETHALITY
A. Cleveland Elementary School
Shooting, Stockton, CA.
On January 17, 1989, a shooter wielding assault
weapons killed five children at their elementary school
and wounded 30 others.22  At the time, the shooting
was the worst school massacre in U.S. history.23  The
capacity and capability of the assault weapons allowed
the shooter to fire over 100 rounds of ammunition
within three minutes.24  Julia Schardt was a second -
grade teacher at the school when the shooting
occurred.
1. Julia Schardt.
At the time of the shooting, Julia Schardt was
inside while her students were at recess.  She
remembers believing that she was hearing the sound
of firecrackers, only later learning that the noises were
gunshots from assault weapons wielded against six- to

nine-year-olds.  One student had stayed inside with a
cold, and Julia recalls grabbing her hand to try to rush
towards safety but ultimately waiting in the classroom
for her other students.  It was then that she heard
another teacher yell, “Oh my God, they are killing our
kids.”  After the shots stopped, there was silence before
her students began to enter the classroom in their
typical single -file fashion.  Julia recalls the chilling
words one student uttered:  “Teacher, Oeun is dead.”
Julia did not want to believe it.  She took roll and
realized two students had not returned, including
Oeun.  But Julia, wanting to provide some comfor t to
the children who had just witnessed the mass murder
of their friends , read them a story.  She remembers
that the children were immobilized—no squirming or
chattering like on a typical day.  The principal soon
checked in over the intercom, and Julia reported her
two missing students.  That conversation was
interrupted when one student remarked that another
was bleeding—the result of ricocheting shrapnel—and
the injured second-grader was carried to the office by
a classroom aide.
Nothing could have prepared Julia for her next task
of that terrible day , accompanying  police to identify
the body of a young student.  Julia was asked to look
at the body of an eight -year-old and match it to the
name of an unaccounted -for child .  It was  Julia’s
student Oeun.  Julia recounts that Oeun’s beautiful
face was marred by a massive head wound where a
bullet had entered her right temple and exited the left
side of her head.  A great deal of blood streaked across

10

her forehead.  Although Julia knew it was Oeun, she
dreaded being the one to officially identify her.
Julia remembers other harrowing accounts from
that day.  She later learned that her other missing
student, Tokla, was transported to the hospital for a
bullet wound that shattered her leg at the hip.  A firstgrader—the best friend of Julia’s son—was shot in his
foot and chest; he almost died.  A third-grader had run
to try to re -enter the school building as bullets flew ,
but found the door locked so was forced to watch in
terror as his friend was killed in front of him.  Older
students had been waiting for lunch at the time of the
shooting and watched as younger children were shot.
A fellow teacher was wounded trying to protect the
children while the shooter fired over 100 rounds.  In
Julia’s view, the assault weapons used allowed for so
much carnage in so little time.  She believes it is hard
to understand the damage the se weapons can do to a
child’s body without seeing it with your own eyes.
Julia and her surviving students were forever
changed by the massacre.  One of the second -graders
repeated to Julia throughout the rest of the school year
that he felt responsible for not saving classmates that
were killed.   This once-promising student has
struggled significantly in adulthood.   Other students
moved away from the town to escape the memories of
that day.  Five students never got the chance ,
including Oeun, whose life ended at only eight -yearsold.  Julia will always remember Oeun as the bright
young girl she was then and will never forget  sitting
with Oeun’s family after the shooting.

B. Pittsburgh Synagogue Shooting.
Shortly before 10 a .m. on Saturday, October 27,

Pittsburgh’s Squirrel Hill neighborhood. 25  Several
groups were meeting in the building that morning. 26
By the time the shooter was apprehended over an hour
later, he had killed 11 and wounded six others,
including four police officers, with a high-powered AR-
15 rifle.27

When the shooter entered the building that

doctor, and his close friend, Dan Leger, a 70 -year-old
retired pediatric nurse and active hospital chaplain,
instinctively went towards the gunfire, hoping to

1. Dan Leger.
Dan Leger was at the Tree of Life Synagogue on
October 27 to attend the Dor Hadash prayer service
and Torah study group.  Shortly before 10 a .m., Dan
and Jerry were preparing for the morning in a study
room.
They suddenly heard a sound “that either sounded
like something blowing things up or gunshots.”  When
Dan realized they were gunshots, he wanted to reach
the lobby’s phone to call the police; he did not carry his
cell phone  on Shabbat.  He also wanted to warn
another congregation meeting downstairs.
He had no time.  As soon as they exited the study,
Jerry looked at Dan and said, “Oh, Dan.”  Dan had no
understanding of what was happening, but he and
Jerry had both been shot.  Dan hopes his was the last
face Jerry saw.  Dan himself had not seen the shooter
or his gun.
Dan remembers falling on a set of stairs “with my
head towards the top and my feet at the bottom” of the
stairs.  He faced a wall and could see very little.  Dan
wears hearing aids, and without a clear view of the

13

scene, spent the next 45 minutes not sure what was
happening.
During that time, Dan thought he was dying .  As
he lay on the stairwell, Dan reviewed his life and
prayed.  He asked God for forgiveness and reflected on
“all of the good that I had experienced:  my kids, my
wife.”
Eventually, Dan heard footsteps.  He describes a
moment of decision:  “I said to myself, if it’s the shooter
he will finish the job, and that’s fine.  I’m going to die
anyways.”  Dan grabbed the pant leg of the person on
the stairs —a paramedic —and remembers hearing,
“this one is alive!”
He was not sure where he had been shot, but felt
intense pressure in his abdomen.  He later learned
that he was shot in the abdomen , with damage to his
hip.  He had suffered massive internal bleeding
forming a tamponade —which involves the internal
build-up of fluid (in Dan’s case, blood). 28  The
tamponade had prevented him from bleeding out
externally.
Dan next remembers “waking up and the figure
above me had this gauzy aspect.”  He thought it was a
member of the Chevra Kadisha, a group of Jewish
adults that traditionally prepares the deceased for

Dan’s recovery was long with several surgeries,
transfusions, and therapy to learn basic life skills
again, including how to eat.  Healing was not linear
and Dan returned to the hospital several more times

After many years working as a nurse, being the patient

Dan had “a really hard time” with the shooter’s

finds it “inconceivable” that people like the shooter
have access to “essentially a machine gun,” and likens

Dan refuses to let his anger get the best of him.  He
emphasizes the support of his community and the
strength he drew from family, friends, and other
survivors.  He often thinks of those murdered in the

Miri Rabinowitz first met Jerry Rabinowitz, a
family physician, in 1993 at a Yom Kippur “breakfast.”  That night, Miri called her best friend and told
her that she had met the man she was going to marry.

Saturday morning services and Torah study.
On October 27, Jerry rose early to complete his
medical rounds before heading to the synagogue.  Miri
rose later and was at home when, around 10 a.m., she
received a call about a shooting at the Tree of Life

Too shaken to drive, Miri called family friends to
drive her there.  Miri recalls learning that “Jer and
Dan [Leger] were still in the building and had not come
out,” and became aware that ambulances had already
left for the hospitals.  Miri began calling other area
hospitals for news of Jerry.  By noon, Miri learned that
Jerry was not among those hospitalized and “knew
that the unaccounted for were deceased.”  By early
afternoon—although unconfirmed—“it was clear to me
that Jerry was dead.”

gathering at a Jewish community center where the

those affected by the shooting.  Around 7:00 p .m., a

community’s Chevra Kadisha had arrived at the Tree

While she still experiences joy, she acknowledges “a
void and a whole part of me that’s gone.”
Although the nature of the weapon or Jerry’s

learned during the trial that the shooter used an
assault weapon, which she describes as “killing

“anti-gun,” but asks what recreational or sporting

C. Oregon District Shooting, Dayton,
OH.
On August 4, 2019, just after midnight, a gunman
went on a rampage in a popular nightlife district in
Dayton, Ohio.  The area —known as the Oregon
District—was a young neighborhood with local shops,
bars, and restaurants.  The gunman, armed with an
assault rifle with a 100 round magazine, body armor,
and a mask, fired 41 shots in just 32 seconds before he
was killed by police.  The attack left nine dead and 27
wounded.31
Dion Green and his father, Derrick Fudge, were
among those trapped in the massacre.  Derrick died.
1. Dion Green.
“I still don’t understand why he didn’t kill me that
night.”  Dion Green was supposed to be celebrating
with his family on the night of August 3, 2019.  Dion’s
home had been devastated by a tornado earlier that

2. Wayne Jones.
“I never thought in a million years I’d see a video of
my mother getting killed.”  For much of her life,
Celestine Chaney was a survivor.  She was a single
mother who raised her only son, Wayne Jones.  They
often went shopping together, stopping at multiple
stores to find the best deal.  On May 14, 2022 ,
Celestine went to Tops in search of shortcake for her
strawberries, accompanied by her older sister.
Celestine was in a festive mood, having just celebrated
her 65 th birthday and recently been declared cancer -
free.  But i t was not cancer —nor the multiple brain
surgeries for aneur ysms that she had suffered—that
killed Celestine.  It was an 18-year-old armed with an
assault weapon.
Wayne was at home watching a movie when he
learned of the shooting.  He could not reach Celestine.
He drove to Tops “just to see if she was in the crowd
and lost her phone.”  Police informed Wayne that all
survivors had left the building and been taken to the
police station or the hospital.  Wayne decided to go
back home to wait to hear from Celestine.
Wayne was home for less than 30 minutes when his
daughter called and alerted him to a Facebook video

25

posted by the shooter livestreaming the entire attack.
Wayne played the video and immediately saw his
mother on the floor.  He watched as the shooter shot
her, ran out of ammunition, and then —after noticing
that Celestine was still moving—quickly reloaded his
assault weapon and shot her again.
The horror of watching his mother die—in a video
filmed by her killer —is almost too unspeakable to
bear.  “I wouldn’t wish anybody would have to see
that.”  Years later, the cold and detached nature of the
shooter’s actions have stuck with Wayne:  “It seemed
like, to him, it was a video game —some virtual
reality.”  But it was real.
Wayne had no time to grieve.  A father of six
children, he immediately went into “parent mode,”
helping his children mourn the loss of their
grandmother, coordinating family travel, and
organizing her funeral services.  After the chaos
following Celestine’s death subsided, Wayne felt deep
loneliness.  “My wife, my daughters, they come and cry
on my shoulders.  But who I always went to, my mom,
she was gone.”
Four years later, Wayne is still in “parent mode.”
He mourns what his children lost that day, the
“granny love” that warms so many children ’s hearts.
He still searches for answers as to why this happened
to him and his family.
Wayne reflected on the weapon that killed his
mother: “There really is no reason for assault weapons.

You don’t shoot anything but other humans with them.

his body was so destroyed from the shots that an open
casket funeral would be impossible.  Through all of

31

this, Jessica was still “trying to comprehend that the
person I love is gone.”
Jessica later watched the recording of the
livestream from the shooter’s phone.  “Watching the
shooter walk up and down the hallway with that gun.
He never could have done the damage that he did if he
didn’t have that gun, that kind of gun.   Josh didn’t
stand a chance—he tried to run.”
The emotional toll on Josh’s family cannot be
understated.  Jessica knows that Josh was her
“person,” the love of her life  whom she got just ten
short years with.  Their children are in therapy,
constantly afraid to go to school or for their mother to
go to work, knowing that work is where their father
was killed.  “The impact never quits.  We’ve never
really gotten to stable ground.”  Jessica cannot enjoy a
happy moment or milestone in the children’s lives
without thinking about Josh missing it.  Josh lived for
his kids; he was there for everything —volunteering,
attending games—and was involved with the church.
Josh was sensitive, thoughtful, and wore his heart on
his sleeve.  He kept a journal of notes he wrote to his
kids to give them when they were older.  Because of an
assault weapon in the hands of a civilian , they will
never know what else he would have shared with him.
F. Assault on First Responders,
Burnsville, MN.
In the early morning o f February 18, 2024, in
Burnsville, Minnesota, firefighter-paramedic Adam

32

Finseth responded to a domestic violence call .  Inside
the home, a man had barricaded himself with seven
children, ages two to fifteen.43  He was armed with two
AR-15 style weapons, one fitted with a binary trigger,44
which fires one round when the trigger is pulled and
another when the trigger is released, delivering twice
the rounds—and damage—in the same amount of
time.45  The shooter released two barrages of fire on
the responding SWAT and Emergency Action team,
ultimately firing  over 100 rounds, killing Adam and
two police off icers and wounding another, before
turning a gun on himself.46  Adam’s sister, Amber, and

1. Brad and Amber Finseth.
Adam Finseth was a veteran who served two tours
of duty  while in the Army, survived cancer, and
worked as a paramedic during the COVID -19
pandemic.  He joined the Burnsville Fire Department
because he felt called to keep serving others .  A
veteran, sportsman, and hunter , Adam believed that
assault weapons belong only with the military.  He had
been trained to use them and understood the damage
they cause.  Amber still cannot believe that , after
everything he survived, he was killed by an assault
weapon in his own community while trying to save
someone else’s life.  “He lived through so many dangers
from the age of 20, only to be killed on American soil,
where assault weapons have become all too easy to
access.”
Brad remembers their last night together after a
family gathering on the Saturday after his birthday.
“Adam and I sat outside, had one last beer, hung out ,
and went to bed.”  “And then it was a nightmare.”  At
7:00 a.m. Sunday, Adam’s wife banged on the door
shouting, “Brad, it’s Adam.”  The family’s lives turned
“upside down.”  Adam and Amber’s mother called
Amber that morning and just said, “Adam is gone.”  “I
remember screaming.”  While in the hospital, Brad

34

asked to just touch the gurney Adam laid in, but was
stopped by a Burnsville liaison, who explained that
“technically he is evidence.”  The rest of that week was
a blur.
Because other mass shooting s with assault
weapons remind them of  Adam’s murder, the family
generally avoids the news .  Still, they think every
family that joins them in this loss is bound by a sorrow
none of them chose.
Adam’s loss reaches beyond his family.  He gave
years to the military before serving as an EMT and
firefighter-paramedic, treating strangers through the
pandemic.  Adam cannot be replaced.  His community
lost a trusted neighbor who had committed his life t o
helping others.   As one detective told Amber, even
when shots started to ring out again and first
responders were shouting at Adam to get to safety, he
continued to provide care to those who had already
been shot —looking out for others before himself.
Adam died alongside two police officers, and their
families and communities share in this loss.
Adam was always there for his family and friends ,
patient and understanding with people no matter how
different they were.  They miss his advice, the way he
made people feel, and how he was the  “constant
guiding light” to those around him.   They miss his
laugh and his hugs, which they heard and felt for the
last time the night before the shooting.  Gathered at
Adam’s family lake cabin, they feel his absence most.

35

They grieve for the life he does not get to live.  Amber
reflects, “He was just getting started.”
CONCLUSION
The threat of violence from the uniquely
destructive force of assault weapons looms over all
aspects of American life.  It ravages communities and
threatens those exercising their faith, spending time
with their families, at their schools, their public
spaces, their jobs, and their comfort and safety every
day.  Amici urge this Court to consider their stories :
the real life, human impact of putting assault weapons
into the hands of civilians.  The Court should preserve
governments’ ability to enact appropriate measures
that limit the havoc wreaked by these assault
weapons.
